extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and American revolutionary history; general readers interested in press history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes evaluative principles, production practices, and rhetorical strategies exemplified by colonial American newspapers (especially patriot organs like the Boston Gazette) during the pre-Revolutionary period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing a political viewpoint (patriotic organ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper that 'would more fairly represent the point of view of the Whigs' and serve as a 'patriotic organ' to counteract Loyalist efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Providence Gazette established to represent Whig viewpoint; editors and contributors wrote explicitly to 'build the paper up as a patriotic organ' and to 'arouse the men of the colony' to sympathy with Boston. Use of partisan editorial line to counteract opposition is presented as a purposeful production choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courageous and able editors/printers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should be 'courageous and able' — willing to risk threats and attacks to publish political content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Benjamin Edes and John Gill, whose office was 'headquarters of the patriots' and who were 'threatened' and 'paid liberally' by opponents; papers sometimes had contributors threatened or mobbed. Courage in editorial stance and personal risk-taking is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industriousness of contributors/editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should demonstrate 'remarkable industry' — persistent, sustained work producing content night after night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samuel Adams is repeatedly described as 'the most industrious, the most effective and the most able of the men writing for the papers,' writing late into the night and constantly furnishing copy and suggestions to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish despite censorship or legal pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should print 'all the news, even if opposed by an "arbitrary power"' and continue publication in defiance of stamps or suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New Hampshire Gazette continued to be published 'as usual without stamps' during the Stamp Act; such defiance is portrayed as a mark of journalistic principle and civic duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as organizing platform/headquarters
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper office functions as an organizing center—'headquarters of the patriots'—where leaders meet, plan, and coordinate political action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston Gazette's back room was used to plan the Boston Tea Party; offices served as spaces for editorial councils, monitoring public sentiment, and circulating documents to towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anonymity and pseudonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often 'seldom, if ever, published anything under his own name' and used numerous 'noms de plume' to carry controversies and influence public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samuel Adams used many disguises (listed examples like 'An American', 'Vindex', 'Populus') to write serial controversies and to shield individual identity while advancing political aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative editorial process (editorial council)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing involved collaborative practices: editors and contributors 'watched the public sentiment... went over the proofs... went through what to-day would be considered an editorial council.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes contributors and leaders meeting in the office to review proofs and coordinate content. Implies editorial judgment, curation, and collective strategy were central to influential papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide distribution and reprinting for impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Content should be readily reprinted and widely circulated — pieces 'were reprinted throughout the colonies' — to maximize influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Warren's oration and the 'Novanglus' letters were widely reprinted; newspapers functioned by exchanging and disseminating material across towns and colonies, amplifying reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artful rhetorical framing to mobilize public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism as 'artful'—use incidents and framing (e.g., the Boston Massacre) to inflame and arouse the public mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samuel Adams' handling of the Boston Massacre is called 'artful journalism'; the account shows use of speeches, review pieces, and moral appeals to provoke public reaction and shape the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter-like, eyewitness court and trial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Good journalism entails being 'always in the court', 'followed the trial carefully, consistently taking notes' and printing informed reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams acted as a 'consummate reporter' for trials, producing informed commentary ('Vindex')—demonstrating value of first-hand observation and detailed reporting in persuasive journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish substantive essays, pamphlets, and legal/political argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should carry serious essays and pamphlets advancing legal, philosophical and political arguments (quoting Montesquieu, Blackstone, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Gazette printed John Adams' 'Canon and Feudal Law' and other weighty pieces; newspapers served as forums for intellectual engagement and attempts to 'find a legal basis' for political action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print primary correspondence and official proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing letters and proposals (e.g., letters to Franklin; suggestions for a 'CONGRESS OF AMERICAN STATES') is a key function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams printed long letters and proposals in the Gazette (e.g., the call for a congress and Bill of Rights), using newspapers to present actionable political plans to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing quality and handling affect credibility and survival
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical quality of printing and handling ('not as well handled or printed as the Gazette') influences a paper's success and longevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portsmouth Mercury succumbed in three years partly because it was 'not as well handled or printed as the Gazette'; production values and editorial competence matter for influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant circulation confers political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: High local readership ('seven-eighths of the people of Boston read no paper but the Boston Gazette') translates directly into political power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hutchinson and royalists attempted to build rival papers by subsidizing contributors, recognizing that circulation numbers determined which arguments shaped public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to present complex or unpopular positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should publish balanced or even unpopular legal defenses and arguments (e.g., Warren and John Adams defended soldiers despite popular feeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing nuanced defenses (John Adams' legal defense in the Massacre trials) is presented as part of responsible journalism able to influence civic judgment rather than merely inflame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of newspapers to form and propagate political platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers print instructions, 'platforms of the Province', committee papers and platforms that travel to all towns, functioning as the province's political platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams' instructions printed by the Gazette circulated through Massachusetts towns and the Committee of Correspondence used the paper to organize more than eighty towns; newspapers acted as tools for political coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting and educating readership with philosophical and legal authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should educate readers by quoting and discussing authorities (Montesquieu, Locke, Blackstone) to support arguments and raise political awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes wide readership of legal and philosophical writers in the colonies and the Gazette's role in disseminating such material even in 'the wilderness', enhancing the intellectual underpinning of political movements.
